overview.text: Mercury (Hg), atomic number 80, is a naturally occurring metal distinguished by being liquid at ordinary room temperatures: it freezes at about −38.8 °C, so it stays liquid around 20 °C. Its shiny silver appearance and high density (about 13.5 g/cm³) make it recognizable; its old name, quicksilver, reflects its silvery, flowing look. Mercury is historically important because its ability to form amalgams with gold helped recover gold from ores, and liquid mercury was used in thermometers and electrical devices. It is seldom found as free metal in nature; it is chiefly obtained from cinnabar ore. Elemental mercury can evaporate into harmful vapor, while methylmercury and other compounds are chemically different forms with distinct exposure risks.

key_facts.text: Mercury’s chemical symbol is Hg and its atomic number is 80.
It is a silvery liquid at 20 °C; its melting point is about −38.8 °C and its density is about 13.53 g/cm³.
Mercury rarely occurs uncombined in nature; cinnabar, or mercury sulfide, is a principal ore.
Mercury forms amalgams with metals such as gold; this property has been used to recover gold from ores.
Elemental mercury can evaporate into toxic vapor. Methylmercury is a different chemical form, so mercury’s health effects depend in part on which form is involved.
